A section groups default content and blocks. Authors add a break with three hyphens (---) on a line of their own; in Google Docs a horizontal line also works.
A block is authored as a table whose merged first row names it. The cells carry content, settings or references, and the block’s code decides how to use them. Which blocks exist de
A variant is written in parentheses after the block name, such as Columns (dark, wide). Each one becomes an extra CSS class on the block, which developers use to change its layout

The Metadata table has the word Metadata in its first row, then one row per property: name on the left, value on the right. It becomes tags in the page head and never appears in th
Auto-blocking turns default content and metadata into blocks, with no table in the document. It runs very early in page decoration, before blocks load, and creates the same structu

The HTTP API at admin.hlx.page for preview, publish, status, code, cache, index, log, config, sitemap and job operations.
The GitHub app that syncs a repository's branches to the Code Bus whenever you push.
A browser extension authors use to preview, publish and unpublish document-based content.
Adobe Experience Manager's web content management product. Edge Delivery Services is part of AEM Sites and requires an AEM Sites licence.
Live domain for Edge Delivery Services sites, formerly hlx.live. Also the home of the official documentation.
Preview domain for Edge Delivery Services sites, formerly hlx.page.

items.t: AODA (Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act)
items.x: Ontario law requiring organizations to meet accessibility standards; for websites the benchmark is WCAG 2.0 AA.
The service that previews and publishes content: it pulls from the content source into the Content Bus and promotes content to live.
Code that turns default content and metadata into blocks early in page decoration.
A component authored as a table whose first row names it; code in blocks/<name>/ decorates it on the page.
Adobe's starter repository for EDS projects, with aem.js, scripts.js, styles and sample blocks.
A URL of the form {ref}--{site}--{org}.aem.page that serves one code branch, so every branch is its own environment.
A sheet that applies metadata to pages by URL pattern.
Using your own production CDN (Akamai, Fastly, Cloudflare or CloudFront) in front of EDS instead of the Adobe-managed CDN.
A content source option where your own service supplies HTML that EDS ingests.
A network of edge servers that caches and serves content close to visitors.
A variation tested against the current experience, the control.
Adobe's console for AEM as a Cloud Service programs and pipelines; since 2026.4.0 it can create Edge Delivery sites.
A score for how much visible content moves unexpectedly while a page loads. Good is 0.1 or less.
Storage for JavaScript, CSS and other code, kept per branch so each branch is its own environment.
Field definitions that drive the Universal Editor Properties panel.
Storage for site and organization configuration, which can inherit from a profile.
The Admin API-backed service that stores organization, profile and site configuration, enabling repoless sites.
Storage for previewed and published content (text, PDFs, SVGs, redirects), with preview and publish lifecycle states.
A structured, reusable piece of content in AEM defined by a model; it can be published to EDS as semantic HTML.
The system where authors create content for an EDS site: AEM with Universal Editor, Google Drive, SharePoint, Document Authoring or a bring-your-own-markup source.
Google's three user-experience metrics: LCP for loading, CLS for visual stability and INP for responsiveness.
Headings, paragraphs, lists, images and links written with normal formatting, outside any block.
The third loading phase: third-party tags, consent and analytics, loaded well after LCP.
AEM's caching and load-balancing module that sits in front of the traditional AEM publish tier.
A browser-based, document-style editor at da.live built for EDS. Adobe now presents it as Experience Workspace.
The first loading phase: everything needed to reach LCP, including the first section and the LCP candidate.
Edge Delivery Services feature stage where a capability is available to customers but may still change significantly and need extra support.
Adobe's edge-rendered publishing and delivery service for websites, part of AEM Sites. It turns authored content into fast, semantic HTML served from a CDN.
JavaScript's native module system (import and export), which browsers load without a build step.
Adobe's newer name and expanded authoring surface for Document Authoring, adding a visual canvas, AI assistance and MCP connections.
A local font sized to match a web font so text does not jump (CLS) when the web font loads after LCP.
A block that places a separately published piece of content on a page.
A later internal project name for Edge Delivery Services, used publicly as "AEM Franklin" before the October 2023 rename.
The older in-repository file that mapped a site to its content source. With the configuration service (Helix 5) it is no longer required.
A content system that stores structured content and delivers it as JSON through APIs, leaving rendering to a separate front end.
Internal Adobe project name behind the technology that became Edge Delivery Services; it survives in names such as hlx.page and admin.hlx.page.
Links equivalent pages across languages, generated through the sitemap on EDS.
Time from a user interaction to the next visual update. Good is 200 milliseconds or less.
An Edge Delivery Services overlay that renders EDS-friendly HTML pages from JSON data at any endpoint.
The second loading phase: project-controlled resources served mostly from the same origin, such as later sections and remaining images.
Time until the largest image or text block in the viewport is painted. Good is 2.5 seconds or less.
Google's lab tool that scores page performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO from 0 to 100. EDS targets 100 on mobile.
The published stage of content, served on an .aem.live host and through the production CDN.
Content kept in sync with its source by Multi Site Manager.
An open protocol that lets AI tools connect to systems such as AEM to read and manage content.
Content-addressable storage for images and media. Each asset is stored once under a hash with a media_ prefix, so it is immutable and can be cached permanently.
AEM's feature for managing live copies of content across sites and locales. With EDS it is combined with repoless setups.
A robots value that keeps a page out of search results and the sitemap.
Google's service that runs Lighthouse and reports field data. The AEM GitHub bot runs it on pull requests.
Configuration that relates AEM content paths to public URLs.
The total bytes a page downloads. aem.live advises keeping the payload before LCP under 100 KB.
Site-wide strings kept in a sheet with Key and Text columns.
The review stage of content, served on an .aem.page host after an author previews a page.
A configuration-service object holding reusable settings (headers, indexes, metadata) that sites in an organization share. A site has at most one profile.
Automatic purging of CDN caches when content is published, so the CDN can cache for a long time without serving stale pages.
A JSON list of published pages used for lists, feeds, search and filters.
Running several sites from one codebase: only the first site has a GitHub repository; the others point to it through configuration.
An Experience Workspace approval workflow that needs onboarding by Adobe.
Performance data collected from real visitors' browsers. In EDS this is called Operational Telemetry.
A part of a page separated by a horizontal rule (---) in documents; it wraps default content and blocks.
A table inside a section that adds classes, an ID or data attributes to it.
HTML that uses elements for their meaning (headings, lists, main) so browsers, search engines and assistive tech understand it.
A Sidekick extension that lets authors browse and copy blocks.
aem.live guidance that, before LCP, only one host should carry network payload, so early connections to other hosts are avoided.
A group of content changes that are reviewed and released together.
Storage that holds documents and spreadsheets in their authored form. Only the API service can access it.
Code loaded from another company's host, such as tag managers, chat widgets or ad pixels.
AEM's WYSIWYG editor for in-context editing with a properties panel; content is stored in AEM and published to EDS.
The W3C accessibility standard. WCAG 2.2 AA is the common enterprise target.
